## Teaching points

1. The classic triad of pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass is present in fewer than half of ruptured AAAs; the report cites up to 42% being first treated as another abdominal condition.
2. A retroperitoneal hematoma tracking along the psoas can irritate lumbar plexus nerves and mimic appendicitis or ureteric colic, even with a high Alvarado score.
3. 'Stable' vital signs do not exclude rupture: a systolic pressure near 100 mm Hg may be relative hypotension in a treated hypertensive.
4. In older patients, especially male smokers, with abdominal, flank or back pain, look at the aorta with bedside ultrasound before settling on appendicitis or renal colic.
5. A contained rupture can bleed again at any time: involve vascular surgery immediately; EVAR is preferred when the anatomy is suitable.
